section_summary: This section opens with a consular letter and newspaper clipping about alleged foreign attempts to copy Japanese products. It then contains a State Department assessment and most of Consul Richard F. Boyce’s report on Japanese inventive capacity and international trade. The report compares Japan and the United States, examines patents, scientific research and industrial production, and includes excerpts and responses from technical societies. The second enclosure continues beyond page 73.

subfiles.title: Enclosing clipping on “Pirating” of Japanese Products
subfiles.from: Arthur Garrels, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards a newspaper clipping on Japanese gendarmerie concern over foreign inquiries into Japanese products.
subfiles.summary: Garrels forwards the June 27 Japan Advertiser clipping for the Department’s interest.

subfiles.title: Now Foreign Industries Trying to ‘Pirate’ Japanese Products, Gendarmerie Claims
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese military concern that foreign buyers seek product information to copy industrial methods.
subfiles.summary: The clipping describes suspected industrial espionage, possible patent violations and a request for cooperation from Osaka business leaders.

subfiles.title: Assessment of Boyce’s “Japanese Inventive Capacity and Its Effect Upon International Trade”
subfiles.about: Explains the decision to grade Boyce’s report “Very Good” despite its substantial merits.
subfiles.summary: The reviewer calls the report lengthy, unevenly objective and sometimes unsupported by its evidence. The memorandum outlines its argument and notes Boyce’s finding that Japanese scientists contribute to several fields, especially alloy-steel research.

subfiles.title: Voluntary Report Cover and Correction to Pages 35–38
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consulate, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Transmits corrections to the report’s historical yen exchange rates and wealth comparison.
subfiles.summary: The correction revises exchange-rate figures and directs cancellation of lines in the report’s comparison.

subfiles.title: Japanese Inventive Capacity and Its Effect Upon International Trade
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consulate, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Examines how Japanese living conditions, industry, research and foreign assistance affect invention and export competition.
subfiles.summary: Boyce compares Japanese and American domestic markets, wealth, wages and mechanization, then classifies Japanese industries by product and market. He reviews patent statistics, government support, scientific work, foreign experts and patents, and production controls. He concludes that Japan excels in staple goods and some lower-grade technical products, while its limited domestic demand and purchasing power constrain invention of modern equipment. He also credits significant Japanese scientific contributions, particularly in metallurgy.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1: Necessity of Industrial Promotion; Machinery
subfiles.from: T. Yano and K. Shirasaki, Nippon: A Charted Survey of Japan 1936
subfiles.about: Argues for Japanese industrial diversification and surveys the development and limits of domestic machinery production.
subfiles.summary: The excerpts describe overpopulation, scarce resources and dependence on imports as reasons to expand manufacturing and exports. They credit Japanese technical progress while noting continued machinery imports caused by patents, demand beyond domestic capacity and uncertain export markets. The machinery survey covers engines, precision instruments, electrical equipment, textiles and major trade partners.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 2: Some Japanese Activities in Modern Technical and Scientific Investigation
subfiles.from: Various American technical and scientific societies, compiled by Richard F. Boyce
subfiles.about: Collects assessments of Japanese contributions across engineering, natural sciences and medicine.
subfiles.summary: Society responses report limited recognized Japanese contributions in automotive and mechanical engineering, alongside substantial work in botany, bacteriology, chemical engineering, entomology, metallurgy, medicine and radio. The metallurgy material particularly praises Kotaro Honda’s research group and its work on magnetic materials and alloy steels. The medical excerpts discuss Hideyo Noguchi’s research and later correction of his interpretation of yellow fever. The enclosure continues after page 73.
